headline: Consumer Affairs Bureau Rates Great Shouting Evacuations: 2.5 Stars, Could Yell Again
deck: Eighteen-thousand residents remain unaccounted as officials argue over their decibel performance ratings.
article:
The Consumer Affairs Bureau delivered a 2.5-star verdict on the Great Shouting Evacuation, placing it just above total collapse. Eighteen thousand Californians stay missing while evaluators graded the effort like a sandwich shop. Average wait times hit 47 minutes at telegram counters for coordinates, and bicycle couriers delivered only 12 percent of "head west" instructions on schedule.

Chief Evaluator Fiona Bellow noted that ridge-station shouting reached "adequate for three blocks but useless against canyon echoes." One resident complained that volume mattered more than accuracy, wishing for a bullhorn from the start.

A follow-up telegram to councils called for stricter shouting rules after uneven decibel levels bred more confusion than order. The new compliance office now pushes residents to submit grievances at telegram windows, trapping them in endless loops of forms and follow-ups. As daylight fades over emptied neighborhoods, the office keeps printing complaint sheets while citizens wonder whether louder lungs will matter next time.
author: Clarence D. Whistleton, Senior Consumer Affairs Correspondent

oped.title: Hats Off to Mediocrity: Why 2.5 Stars Is Generous
oped.author: Professor Thaddeus Bloviate, Official Telegram Censor and Decibel Laureate
oped.body: The Bureau's 2.5-star rating insults vocal tradition. Those shouters performed without telephones, their voices bouncing between messengers as proper 2026 commerce demands. The real problem rests with the eighteen thousand missing, whose oversized fedoras swallowed every useful syllable. A bylaw forcing hatless drills would fix it. Citizens should also pay for a new corps of shouting inspectors—led by experts such as myself—who will issue daily telegram ratings of lung capacity. Anything less rewards laziness and delays my overdue appointment. If the lost had simply doffed their hats and listened, this endless paperwork would never have begun.

classifieds.text: HELP WANTED: Bureau requires 200 louder yellers for re-evacuation of 18k missing. Telegrams only, no bike messengers with weak lungs.
LOST & FOUND: Seeking 18,000 unaccounted residents after 2.5-star shouting fiasco. Reward one bullhorn if located via telegram.
PUBLIC NOTICE: Officials apologize for subpar decibels; all missing urged to shout their locations to nearest bike messenger before next rating.
PERSONALS: Darling, my yell failed you in the evacuation. Meet at telegram office at dusk, bring stronger voice.

stories.headline: Suburban HOAs Require Residents to Practice Shouting Routes Twice Weekly
stories.deck: Compliance officers now log decibel logs alongside lawn height violations.
stories.article:
Homeowner associations statewide added vocal drills to their rules after the evacuation. Residents must now prove they can shout neighbors toward assembly points before fence permits clear.

A Pasadena board logged a 40 percent jump in noise complaints once evening sessions started. The drills cut minor telegram disputes but sent bicycle couriers racing to deliver throat lozenges.

stories.headline: Telegraph Firms Report Surge in Bulk Disaster Message Contracts
stories.deck: Corporate clients now pre-pay for repeated evacuation wording revisions.
stories.article:
Wire services recorded peak profits once agencies ordered multiple alert drafts for every possible shouting result. One firm added fees for rooftop delivery instead of courier handoff.

Executives blamed the lack of direct calls for bigger messenger fleets parked near county buildings. Several companies now bundle telegram dispatch with later volume checks.

stories.headline: Bike Couriers Charged With Using Evacuation Shouts to Cover Thefts
stories.deck: Suspects allegedly yelled directions while removing items from vacated homes.
stories.article:
Officers in three counties detained messenger teams accused of faking route calls during the alert. Witnesses said the groups shouted assembly points while others hauled electronics into carts.

Prosecutors noted missing phone records slowed the investigation. Departments now demand couriers register standard shout phrases ahead of time with local telegraph offices.
